{{Short description|Theory for associative algebras over rings}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Hochschild homology (and cohomology)''' is a [[homology theory]] for [[associative]] [[algebra (ring theory)|algebras]] over [[ring (mathematics)|rings]]. There is also a theory for Hochschild homology of certain [[functor]]s. Hochschild cohomology was introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink= Gerhard Hochschild|first=Gerhard |last= Hochschild |year=1945}} for algebras over a [[field (mathematics)|field]], and extended to algebras over more general rings by {{harvs|txt|last1=Cartan|first1=Henri|author1-link=Henri Cartan|last2=Eilenberg|first2=Samuel|author2-link=Samuel Eilenberg|year=1956}}.

==Definition of Hochschild homology of algebras==
Let ''k'' be a field, ''A'' an [[associative]] ''k''-[[algebra (ring theory)|algebra]], and ''M'' an ''A''-[[bimodule]]. The enveloping algebra of ''A'' is the tensor product <math>A^e=A\otimes A^o</math> of ''A'' with its [[opposite ring|opposite algebra]]. Bimodules over ''A'' are essentially the same as modules over the enveloping algebra of ''A'', so in particular ''A'' and ''M'' can be considered as ''A<sup>e</sup>''-modules. {{harvtxt|Cartan|Eilenberg|1956}} defined the Hochschild homology and cohomology group of ''A'' with coefficients in ''M''  in terms of the [[Tor functor]] and [[Ext functor]] by

:<math> HH_n(A,M) = \operatorname{Tor}_n^{A^e}(A, M)</math>
:<math> HH^n(A,M) = \operatorname{Ext}^n_{A^e}(A, M)</math>

===Hochschild complex===
Let ''k'' be a ring, ''A'' an [[associative]] ''k''-[[algebra (ring theory)|algebra]] that is a [[projective module|projective]] ''k''-module, and ''M'' an ''A''-[[bimodule]]. We will write <math>A^{\otimes n}</math> for the ''n''-fold [[tensor product]] of ''A'' over ''k''. The [[chain complex]] that gives rise to Hochschild homology is given by

:<math> C_n(A,M) := M \otimes A^{\otimes n} </math>

with boundary operator <math>d_i</math> defined by

:<math>\begin{align}
d_0(m\otimes a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) &= ma_1 \otimes a_2 \cdots \otimes a_n \\
d_i(m\otimes a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) &= m\otimes a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_i a_{i+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n \\
d_n(m\otimes a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) &= a_n m\otimes a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_{n-1} 
\end{align}</math>

where <math>a_i</math> is in ''A'' for all <math>1\le i\le n</math> and <math>m\in M</math>. If we let

:<math> b_n=\sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i d_i, </math>

then <math>b_{n-1} \circ b_{n} =0</math>, so <math>(C_n(A,M),b_n)</math> is a [[chain complex]] called the '''Hochschild complex''', and its homology is the '''Hochschild homology''' of ''A'' with coefficients in ''M''. Henceforth, we will write <math>b_n</math> as simply <math>b</math>.

===Remark===
The maps <math>d_i</math> are [[face map]]s making the family of [[module (mathematics)|modules]] <math>(C_n(A,M),b)</math> a [[Face map#Simplicial objects|simplicial object]] in the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of ''k''-modules, i.e., a functor Δ<sup>o</sup> → ''k''-mod, where Δ is the [[simplex category]] and ''k''-mod is the category of ''k''-modules. Here Δ<sup>o</sup> is the [[Dual (category theory)|opposite category]] of Δ. The [[degeneracy map]]s are defined by

:<math>s_i(a_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) = a_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_i \otimes 1 \otimes a_{i+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n.</math>

Hochschild homology is the homology of this simplicial module.

=== Relation with the bar complex ===
There is a similar looking complex <math>B(A/k)</math> called the [[bar complex]] which formally looks very similar to the Hochschild complex<ref>{{Cite web|last=Morrow|first=Matthew|date=|title=Topological Hochschild homology in arithmetic geometry|url=https://www.math.arizona.edu/~swc/aws/2019/2019MorrowNotes.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224194152/https://www.math.arizona.edu/~swc/aws/2019/2019MorrowNotes.pdf|archive-date=24 Dec 2020|access-date=|website=}}</ref><sup>pg 4-5</sup>. In fact, the Hochschild complex <math>HH(A/k)</math> can be recovered from the bar complex as<math display="block">HH(A/k) \cong A\otimes_{A\otimes A^{op}} B(A/k)</math>giving an explicit isomorphism.

=== As a derived self-intersection ===
There's another useful interpretation of the Hochschild complex in the case of commutative rings, and more generally, for sheaves of commutative rings: it is constructed from the [[Derived scheme|derived self-intersection]] of a [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] (or even derived scheme) <math>X</math> over some base scheme <math>S</math>. For example, we can form the derived [[Fiber product of schemes|fiber product]]<math display="block">X\times^\mathbf{L}_SX</math>which has the sheaf of derived rings <math>\mathcal{O}_X\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_S}^\mathbf{L}\mathcal{O}_X</math>. Then, if embed <math>X</math> with the diagonal map<math display="block">\Delta: X \to X\times^\mathbf{L}_SX</math>the Hochschild complex is constructed as the pullback of the derived self intersection of the diagonal in the diagonal product scheme<math display="block">HH(X/S) := \Delta^*(\mathcal{O}_X\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_S}^\mathbf{L}\mathcal{O}_X}^\mathbf{L}\mathcal{O}_X)</math>From this interpretation, it should be clear the Hochschild homology should have some relation to the Kähler differentials <math>\Omega_{X/S}</math> since the [[Kähler differential|Kähler differentials]] can be defined using a self-intersection from the diagonal, or more generally, the [[cotangent complex]] <math>\mathbf{L}_{X/S}^\bullet</math> since this is the derived replacement for the Kähler differentials. We can recover the original definition of the Hochschild complex of a commutative <math>k</math>-algebra <math>A</math> by setting<math display="block">S = \text{Spec}(k)</math> and <math display="block">X = \text{Spec}(A)</math>Then, the Hochschild complex is [[Quasi-isomorphism|quasi-isomorphic]] to<math display="block">HH(A/k) \simeq_{qiso} A\otimes_{A\otimes_{k}^\mathbf{L}A}^\mathbf{L}A </math>If <math>A</math> is a flat <math>k</math>-algebra, then there's the chain of isomorphisms <math display="block">A\otimes_k^\mathbf{L}A \cong A\otimes_kA \cong A\otimes_kA^{op}</math>giving an alternative but equivalent presentation of the Hochschild complex.

==Hochschild homology of functors==
The [[simplicial circle]] <math>S^1</math> is a simplicial object in the category <math>\operatorname{Fin}_*</math> of finite pointed sets, i.e., a functor <math>\Delta^o \to \operatorname{Fin}_*.</math> Thus, if ''F'' is a functor <math>F\colon \operatorname{Fin} \to k\text{-mod}</math>, we get a simplicial module by composing ''F'' with <math>S^1</math>.

:<math> \Delta^o \overset{S^1}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Fin}_* \overset{F}{\longrightarrow} k\text{-mod}.</math>

The homology of this simplicial module is the '''Hochschild homology of the functor''' ''F''. The above definition of Hochschild homology of [[Associative algebra|commutative algebras]] is the special case where ''F'' is the '''Loday functor'''.

===Loday functor===
A [[skeleton (category theory)|skeleton]] for the category of finite pointed sets is given by the objects

:<math> n_+ = \{0,1,\ldots,n\},</math>

where 0 is the basepoint, and the [[morphism (category theory)|morphisms]] are the basepoint preserving set maps. Let ''A'' be a commutative k-algebra and ''M'' be a symmetric ''A''-bimodule{{Elucidate|date=March 2012}}. The Loday functor <math>L(A,M)</math> is given on objects in <math>\operatorname{Fin}_*</math> by

:<math> n_+ \mapsto M \otimes A^{\otimes n}.</math>

A morphism

:<math>f:m_+ \to n_+</math>

is sent to the morphism <math>f_*</math> given by

:<math> f_*(a_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_m) = b_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_n </math>

where

:<math>\forall j \in \{0, \ldots, n \}: \qquad b_j =
\begin{cases}
\prod_{i \in f^{-1}(j)} a_i & f^{-1}(j) \neq \emptyset\\
1 & f^{-1}(j) =\emptyset
\end{cases}</math>

===Another description of Hochschild homology of algebras===
The Hochschild homology of a commutative algebra ''A'' with coefficients in a symmetric ''A''-bimodule ''M'' is the homology associated to the composition

:<math>\Delta^o \overset{S^1}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Fin}_* \overset{\mathcal{L}(A,M)}{\longrightarrow} k\text{-mod},</math>

and this definition agrees with the one above.

== Examples ==
The examples of Hochschild homology computations can be stratified into a number of distinct cases with fairly general theorems describing the structure of the homology groups and the homology ring <math>HH_*(A)</math> for an associative algebra <math>A</math>. For the case of commutative algebras, there are a number of theorems describing the computations over characteristic 0 yielding a straightforward understanding of what the homology and cohomology compute.

=== Commutative characteristic 0 case ===
In the case of commutative algebras <math>A/k</math> where <math>\mathbb{Q}\subseteq k</math>, the Hochschild homology has two main theorems concerning smooth algebras, and more general non-flat algebras <math>A</math>; but, the second is a direct generalization of the first. In the smooth case, i.e. for a smooth algebra <math>A</math>, the '''Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem'''<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Ginzburg|first=Victor|date=2005-06-29|title=Lectures on Noncommutative Geometry|eprint=math/0506603 }}</ref><sup>pg 43-44</sup> states there is an isomorphism <math display="block">\Omega^n_{A/k} \cong HH_n(A/k)</math> for every <math>n \geq 0</math>. This isomorphism can be described explicitly using the anti-symmetrization map. That is, a differential <math>n</math>-form has the map<math display="block">a\,db_1\wedge \cdots \wedge db_n \mapsto
\sum_{\sigma \in S_n}\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)
    a\otimes b_{\sigma(1)}\otimes \cdots \otimes b_{\sigma(n)}.</math>
If the algebra <math>A/k</math> isn't smooth, or even flat, then there is an analogous theorem using the [[cotangent complex]]. For a simplicial resolution <math>P_\bullet \to A</math>, we set <math>\mathbb{L}^i_{A/k} = \Omega^i_{P_\bullet/k}\otimes_{P_\bullet} A</math>. Then, there exists a descending <math>\mathbb{N}</math>-filtration <math>F_\bullet</math> on <math>HH_n(A/k)</math> whose graded pieces are isomorphic to <math display="block">\frac{F_i}{F_{i+1}} \cong \mathbb{L}^i_{A/k}[+i].</math>
Note this theorem makes it accessible to compute the Hochschild homology not just for smooth algebras, but also for [[Complete intersection ring|local complete intersection]] algebras. In this case, given a presentation <math>A = R/I</math> for <math>R = k[x_1,\dotsc,x_n]</math>, the cotangent complex is the two-term complex <math>I/I^2 \to \Omega^1_{R/k}\otimes_k A</math>.

==== Polynomial rings over the rationals ====
One simple example is to compute the Hochschild homology of a [[polynomial ring]] of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> with <math>n</math>-generators. The HKR theorem gives the isomorphism <math display="block">HH_*(\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]) = \mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]\otimes \Lambda(dx_1,\dotsc, dx_n)</math> where the algebra <math>\bigwedge(dx_1,\ldots, dx_n)</math> is the free antisymmetric algebra over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> in <math>n</math>-generators. Its product structure is given by the [[wedge product]] of vectors, so <math display="block">\begin{align}
dx_i\cdot dx_j &= -dx_j\cdot dx_i \\
dx_i\cdot dx_i &= 0  
\end{align}</math> for <math>i \neq j</math>.

=== Commutative characteristic p case ===
In the characteristic p case, there is a userful counter-example to the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem which elucidates for the need of a theory beyond simplicial algebras for defining Hochschild homology. Consider the <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-algebra <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math>. We can compute a resolution of <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> as the free differential graded algebras<math display="block">\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\cdot p} \mathbb{Z}</math>giving the derived intersection <math>\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p \cong \mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)</math> where <math>\text{deg}(\varepsilon) = 1</math> and the differential is the zero map. This is because we just tensor the complex above by <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math>, giving a formal complex with a generator in degree <math>1</math> which squares to <math>0</math>. Then, the Hochschild complex is given by<math display="block">\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbb{L}_{\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbb{L}_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{F}_p}\mathbb{F}_p</math>In order to compute this, we must resolve <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> as an <math>\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p</math>-algebra. Observe that the algebra structure

<math>\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2) \to \mathbb{F}_p</math>

forces <math>\varepsilon \mapsto 0</math>. This gives the degree zero term of the complex. Then, because we have to resolve the kernel <math>\varepsilon \cdot \mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p</math>, we can take a copy of <math>\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p</math> shifted in degree <math>2</math> and have it map to <math>\varepsilon \cdot \mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p</math>, with kernel in degree <math>3</math><math>\varepsilon \cdot \mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p = \text{Ker}({\displaystyle \mathbb {F} _{p}\otimes _{\mathbb {Z} }^{\mathbf {L} }\mathbb {F} _{p}} \to {\displaystyle \varepsilon \cdot \mathbb {F} _{p}\otimes _{\mathbb {Z} }^{\mathbf {L} }\mathbb {F} _{p}}).</math>We can perform this recursively to get the underlying module of the divided power algebra<math display="block">(\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p)\langle x \rangle = 
\frac{
(\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p)[x_1,x_2,\ldots]
}{x_ix_j = \binom{i+j}{i}x_{i+j}}</math>with <math>dx_i = \varepsilon\cdot x_{i-1}</math> and the degree of <math>x_i</math> is <math>2i</math>, namely <math>|x_i| = 2i</math>. Tensoring this algebra with <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> over <math>\mathbb{F}_p\otimes^\mathbf{L}_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{F}_p</math> gives<math display="block">HH_*(\mathbb{F}_p) = \mathbb{F}_p\langle x \rangle</math>since <math>\varepsilon</math> multiplied with any element in <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> is zero. The algebra structure comes from general theory on divided power algebras and differential graded algebras.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Section 23.6 (09PF): Tate resolutions—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09PF|access-date=2020-12-31|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref> Note this computation is seen as a technical artifact because the ring <math>\mathbb{F}_p\langle x \rangle</math> is not well behaved. For instance, <math>x^p = 0</math>. One technical response to this problem is through Topological Hochschild homology, where the base ring <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is replaced by the [[sphere spectrum]] <math>\mathbb{S}</math>.

==Topological Hochschild homology==
{{Main|Topological Hochschild homology}}
The above construction of the Hochschild complex can be adapted to more general situations, namely by replacing the category of (complexes of) '''<math>k</math>'''-modules by an [[infinity category|∞-category]] (equipped with a tensor product) <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, and '''<math>A</math>''' by an associative algebra in this category. Applying this to the category <math>\mathcal{C}=\textbf{Spectra}</math> of [[spectrum (topology)|spectra]], and '''''<math>A</math>''''' being the [[Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum]] associated to an ordinary ring <math>R</math> yields '''topological Hochschild homology''', denoted <math>THH(R)</math>. The (non-topological) Hochschild homology introduced above can be reinterpreted along these lines, by taking for ''<math>\mathcal{C} = D(\mathbb{Z})</math>'' the [[derived category]] of <math>\Z</math>-modules (as an ∞-category).

Replacing tensor products over the [[sphere spectrum]] by tensor products over <math>\Z</math> (or the Eilenberg–MacLane-spectrum <math>H\Z</math>) leads to a natural comparison map <math>THH(R) \to HH(R)</math>. It induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups in degrees 0, 1, and 2. In general, however, they are different, and '''<math>THH</math>''' tends to yield simpler groups than HH. For example,

:<math>THH(\mathbb{F}_p) = \mathbb{F}_p[x],</math>
:<math>HH(\mathbb{F}_p) = \mathbb{F}_p\langle x \rangle</math>

is the polynomial ring (with ''x'' in degree 2), compared to the ring of [[divided powers]] in one variable.

{{harvs|txt|last=Hesselholt|first=Lars|author-link=Lars Hesselholt|year=2016}} showed that the [[Hasse–Weil zeta function]] of a smooth proper variety over <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> can be expressed using [[functional determinant|regularized determinants]] involving topological Hochschild homology.
